KEEP fixed/variable/total cost definitions and the revenue/profit-per-unit formulas. ADD R067-specific spec quirks: salaries and utilities are classified as fixed (not variable) for this qualification; wages are variable; loan repayments are NOT a cost but loan interest IS — these are common confusions per OCR examiner reports. Calculations must also cover per-unit and per-period (per month/year) variants, plus rearranging formulas, which the spec explicitly requires.

source_lesson.title: Aims, Objectives and Business Calculations
source_lesson.description: Financial and non-financial aims, plus revenue, costs and profit calculations.
source_lesson.content_html:
What Are Aims and Objectives?

Before a business can make decisions about pricing, staffing or marketing, it needs to know what it is trying to achieve. A business aim is a general, long-term goal — something like “become the most trusted bakery in the city” or “survive the first two years of trading.” An objective is a specific, measurable target set to work towards that aim — for example, “increase revenue by 15% over the next 12 months.”

The distinction matters in the exam: aims are broad directions; objectives are the concrete milestones. A business without clear objectives struggles to judge whether it is on track or needs to change course.

Key Fact

Business aims and objectives split into financial (survival, profit, sales, market share, financial security) and non-financial (social objectives, personal satisfaction, challenge, independence and control). Both types matter — especially for sole traders and small businesses where the owner’s personal goals often drive the business.

Financial Aims and Objectives

Survival is typically the number-one priority for a new business. In the first year, cash flow pressures, low customer awareness and unexpected costs can threaten even well-planned ventures. A business focused on survival may accept low or zero profit short-term, just to keep trading.

Profit — the money left over after all costs are deducted from revenue — becomes a primary objective once survival is secured. Profit funds growth, rewards the owner, and provides a buffer against future downturns. Market share refers to a business’s percentage of total sales in its market. Gaining market share often requires investing in marketing or lowering prices, which reduces short-term profit but may build a stronger position over time. Financial security means having enough reserves to absorb shocks — particularly important for seasonal businesses.

Non-Financial Aims and Objectives

Not every entrepreneur is primarily motivated by money. Social objectives might include reducing environmental impact, paying staff above the minimum wage, or donating a proportion of profits to charity. Many small businesses — particularly cooperatives and community enterprises — place social objectives above financial ones.

Other non-financial motivations include personal satisfaction (building something meaningful), challenge (proving a business concept works), and independence and control (being your own boss and making your own decisions). These are common reasons people leave employed work to start a business, even when doing so involves financial risk.

Aims differ because of the business’s age, size, ownership type and the owner’s personal motivations. A new sole trader in year one may focus entirely on survival; the same trader three years later may prioritise profit maximisation or independence. A private limited company with investors is more likely to prioritise financial returns to satisfy shareholders.

External factors also shift objectives. During an economic recession, even profit-focused businesses may downgrade their objective to survival. During a period of growth, a business confident in its cash position may switch to an aggressive market-share target. Understanding why objectives change — and being able to link this to a business context — is an AO2 application skill that earns marks in extended responses.

Revenue, Costs and Profit — The Calculations

Revenue is calculated by multiplying the selling price by the number of units sold:
Revenue = Price × Quantity sold

Costs fall into two types. Fixed costs do not change with the level of output — examples include rent, insurance and management salaries. Even if a business sells nothing in a month, fixed costs still have to be paid. Variable costs change directly with output — raw materials, packaging and sales commission are typical examples. The more you produce, the higher your total variable costs.

Total costs combine both:
Total costs = Total fixed costs + Total variable costs

Key Fact

Profit = Revenue − Total costs. If this figure is negative, the business is making a loss. Profit is NOT the same as cash — a profitable business can still run out of cash if customers pay late or stock builds up.

When a business borrows money, it repays more than it borrowed. The extra amount is called interest. The formula to calculate the interest rate (as a percentage) is:
Interest (%) = ((Total repayment − Amount borrowed) ÷ Amount borrowed) × 100

Example: a business borrows £20,000 and repays £24,000 in total.
Interest = ((24,000 − 20,000) ÷ 20,000) × 100 = (4,000 ÷ 20,000) × 100 = 20%
Interest is a fixed cost for the business and must be covered regardless of how much revenue is generated.

Worked Calculation Example

Foxgrove Candles sells handmade candles at £12 each. In July it sold 800 units. Its fixed costs for July were £3,200 (rent and insurance). Its variable costs were £4.50 per candle.

Revenue: £12 × 800 = £9,600
Total variable costs: £4.50 × 800 = £3,600
Total costs: £3,200 + £3,600 = £6,800
Profit: £9,600 − £6,800 = £2,800
source_lesson.exam_tip_html: For “Define” questions (1 mark), give a precise, single-sentence definition — one sentence covering the key idea. Vague answers such as “profit is when you make money” score zero; “profit is revenue minus total costs” scores the mark. For 2-mark and 3-mark “Calculate” questions, always write the formula first, then substitute the given figures — but remember, the mark goes to the final numerical answer with units (£), not to the formula alone. On 9-mark “Discuss” questions about aims and objectives, avoid generic lists — the higher marks go to students who explain why a specific type of business (e.g. a new sole trader vs an established Ltd) would prioritise one aim over another, with a developed reasoning chain.
source_lesson.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Business aims are long-term directions; objectives are specific measurable targets. Both can be financial (survival, profit, market share) or non-financial (social objectives, independence, challenge).
  • Revenue = Price × Quantity; Total costs = Fixed costs + Variable costs; Profit = Revenue − Total costs. These three formulas must be recalled without a formula sheet in the exam.
  • Cash and profit are not the same thing — a business can be profitable but still run out of cash, which is why cash-flow management is covered as a separate topic.

practice_questions.marks: Revenue is the total money received by a business from selling its products or services, calculated as price multiplied by quantity sold. [1 mark — must include the idea of price × quantity or total income from sales]

practice_questions.text:
A business sells 500 units at a price of £8 each. Its fixed costs are £1,800 and its variable costs are £3 per unit.

Calculate the business's total costs.
practice_questions.marks:
Formula: Total costs = Total fixed costs + Total variable costs
Total variable costs = £3 × 500 = £1,500
Total costs = £1,800 + £1,500 = £3,300 [2 marks for correct final answer of £3,300; allow 1 mark if correct method shown but arithmetic error]

practice_questions.text:
A business borrows £15,000 and repays a total of £18,750 over three years.

Calculate the total interest paid as a percentage of the amount borrowed. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Formula: Interest (%) = ((Total repayment − Amount borrowed) ÷ Amount borrowed) × 100
Substitution: ((18,750 − 15,000) ÷ 15,000) × 100
= (3,750 ÷ 15,000) × 100
= 25%
[3 marks: 1 mark for identifying the interest amount (£3,750); 1 mark for correct division (÷ 15,000); 1 mark for correct final answer of 25%. Allow follow-through from earlier arithmetic errors if method is correct.]

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why a small business owner might have non-financial aims for their business.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 6 marks; only the best two developed points count.

Point 1 — Personal satisfaction/independence:
A business owner may aim for independence and control because they want to make their own decisions rather than following orders from an employer. This non-financial aim reflects a desire for autonomy — the owner values freedom over maximising their salary.

Point 2 — Social objectives:
An owner may aim to benefit the community or environment, for example by using local suppliers or reducing packaging waste. Achieving this social objective may actually reduce profit, but the owner values the social impact of their business more than additional financial return.

Point 3 (if offered) — Personal challenge:
Some entrepreneurs start a business to prove to themselves (and others) that a concept can work. The challenge of building something from scratch is motivating in itself, even if financial rewards are limited in the short term.

1 mark per basic statement of fact; +1 for logical development; +1 for a further step that extends the point. No context required for Explain questions.

practice_questions.text:
Saltwick Press is a small independent bookshop in a seaside town. The owner, Fiona, set it up three years ago. In year one, her only aim was to survive. Now that the business is profitable, she is considering whether to focus on maximising profit or to expand her social media presence and run community reading events that may not directly increase sales.

Discuss whether Fiona should change her business objectives now that Saltwick Press is established.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (8–9 marks): Extended, analytical discussion of financial and non-financial objectives with clear reasoning about why a business's objectives evolve over time. May bring in the bookshop context (seasonal trade, community ties, independent vs online retail competition). Reaches a developed judgement about which direction is more appropriate for this type of business, backed by reasoning.

Secure (5–7 marks): Discusses both financial and non-financial objectives with some developed reasoning. May not fully contextualise within the bookshop scenario but reasoning about the trade-off between profit and social objectives is present.

Developing (3–4 marks): Identifies financial and non-financial aims with basic development. Limited connection to how or why objectives change as a business matures.

Emerging (1–2 marks): Lists types of aims with little or no analysis of the trade-off or context.

practice_questions.text:
Brightside Fitness is a start-up gym with 120 members. It charges £35 per month. Monthly fixed costs are £2,800. Variable costs are £5 per member per month.

Calculate Brightside Fitness's monthly profit.
practice_questions.marks:
Formula: Profit = Revenue − Total costs
Revenue = £35 × 120 = £4,200
Total variable costs = £5 × 120 = £600
Total costs = £2,800 + £600 = £3,400
Profit = £4,200 − £3,400 = £800
[3 marks: 1 mark for correct revenue (£4,200); 1 mark for correct total costs (£3,400); 1 mark for correct profit figure (£800). Allow follow-through on arithmetic errors if method is clear.]

glossary_terms.definition: A broad statement of what a business wants to achieve in the long term.
A specific, measurable target that helps a business work towards its broader aim.
The total money received by a business from selling its products or services; calculated as price multiplied by quantity sold.
Business objectives related to benefiting society, the community or the environment rather than maximising financial returns.
Business costs that do not change with the level of output, such as rent and insurance, and must be paid even if nothing is produced.
Costs that rise and fall directly with the level of output, such as raw materials and packaging.
The money left over after total costs are deducted from revenue; a key financial aim for most businesses.
A business's sales expressed as a percentage of total sales in its market; gaining market share means growing faster than rivals.
